title: API 580 Training in Chicago: RBI Exam Prep Online
description: API 580 exam prep for Chicago-area RBI teams: PSM programmes at Whiting, Joliet and Morris, crude slate changes, lakefront consequence, self-paced online.
h1: API 580 training in Chicago: preparing integrity engineers and inspection planners for the risk-based inspection examination
html:
API 580 exam prep for RBI teams across Chicagoland

Risk-based inspection is how the big plants around Chicago decide where their inspection hours go. A refinery the size of Whiting cannot open every drum, gauge every circuit and scan every tank floor on a fixed calendar, so its integrity group ranks equipment by the probability and the consequence of failure and spends effort where the risk is. The API 580 certification shows that the person building or auditing that ranking understands the method API RP 580 sets out: what data it needs, which damage mechanisms drive it, how inspection changes it and how the results must be documented.

Atlantis NDT's API 580 course prepares candidates for that examination. You study online at your own pace, and an instructor answers the questions RP 580 raises along the way. There is no Atlantis classroom in Chicago, and none is needed for a closed-book paper that rewards reading and rehearsal. The American Petroleum Institute sets eligibility, administers the examination and issues the certification; you apply to API yourself.

Who sits API 580 around Chicago

The candidates are rarely new to inspection. Around Whiting, Joliet, Lemont and the chemical plants of the Illinois River corridor they tend to be:

  • Inspection planners and inspection supervisors who turn the RBI output into the work list for the next run and the next turnaround;
  • Reliability, corrosion and materials engineers who assign damage mechanisms, set corrosion rates and argue for or against interval changes;
  • API 510, 570 and 653 inspectors who want the RBI credential to sit beside their code certificate, and who qualify for API 580 automatically while their certificate is current;
  • Process safety and mechanical integrity coordinators who need to defend the inspection programme to auditors and regulators.

Without a current inspector certification, API combines education with petrochemical industry experience gained in the last ten years: one year with a bachelor's degree, two with a two-year degree, three with a high school diploma and five or more with no formal education. A process engineer at an olefins plant or a terminal integrity specialist may therefore qualify without ever having held API 510.

PSM mechanical integrity on both sides of the state line

Most of the large Chicago-area units handle highly hazardous chemicals above the threshold quantities in OSHA's process safety management standard, 29 CFR 1910.119. Its mechanical integrity paragraph covers pressure vessels and storage tanks, piping and its valves, relief and vent systems, emergency shutdown systems, controls and pumps. It requires inspections and tests that follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices, at a frequency consistent with manufacturers' recommendations and good practice, and more often where operating experience shows the need. Each inspection must be documented with its date, the inspector's name, the equipment identifier, a description of the work and the results.

That frequency requirement is where RBI earns its place. An interval set by a documented risk assessment that follows RP 580 is one way an owner shows its frequencies are consistent with good engineering practice. Enforcement differs across the metro: in Illinois, private employers fall under federal OSHA, because the state plan covers only state and local government workers, while Indiana's state plan, run by IOSHA within the Indiana Department of Labor, covers private workplaces such as the refinery at Whiting. The standard is the same text either way, but an RBI programme serving a company with sites in both states answers to two inspectorates.

When the crude changes, the risk changes

The clearest local lesson in why RBI is a living assessment is the change in what Chicago refineries run. Oil & Gas Journal reported that after Whiting's 2013 modernization, heavy, sour crude including Canadian bitumen could make up more than 80% of the feed, against about 20% before, and ExxonMobil says Joliet runs Canadian crude delivered by pipeline. A feed change of that size moves the probability side of the assessment for whole units. Sulfidation and naphthenic acid corrosion in hot sections, overhead chloride corrosion and hydrogen damage in hydroprocessing all depend on the feed, so their susceptibility, rates and inspection effectiveness assumptions have to be revisited.

RP 580 expects an assessment to be updated when the process, the operating conditions or the equipment change, and after inspections add data. For an exam candidate the point is conceptual, and it is examined in the data collection, damage mechanism and risk management areas of the Body of Knowledge. For a Chicago integrity group it is practical: a crude slate change, a new unit or a revised operating window should trigger a review of the affected items, and the record should show it happened.

Consequence beside a lake, a river and a canal

Consequence of failure is where a Chicago RBI model differs most from a remote Gulf Coast example. The region's big sites sit next to water and people:

  • bp's Whiting refinery is one of the Lake Michigan sites of interest the Indiana Department of Environmental Management tracks, with its own discharge permit, and it sits in the city of Whiting beside Hammond and East Chicago;
  • ExxonMobil describes its Joliet refinery as lying 40 miles south-west of Chicago near Interstate 55 and the Des Plaines River, with a barge loading dock on site;
  • Kinder Morgan's Argo terminal, with 218 tanks and about 2.67 million barrels of storage, sits on the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, and its Chicago terminal on the Calumet River and Lake Calumet.

RP 580 treats consequence as more than flammability. Safety, environmental and business consequences can all be assessed, and an item whose leak would reach a river, a canal or Lake Michigan can rank high even with a modest probability of failure. Exam questions on consequence often turn on which factors increase it (inventory, release rate, detection and isolation, the surroundings) and which actions reduce it. Inspection is not one of them.

Tank farms and breakout tanks: where RBI is limited

Several of the largest tank fields near Chicago belong to pipelines. Enbridge gives its Griffith terminal in Indiana a shell capacity of 2.8 million barrels and its Hartsdale terminal near Schererville about 1.5 million, and the long-haul crude lines of its Lakehead system terminate in Indiana. Tanks that serve a hazardous liquid pipeline as breakout tanks fall under 49 CFR 195.432, which requires inspection to API Std 653 but excludes its section 6.4.3, the risk-based alternative for setting internal inspection intervals. RBI can still prioritise those tanks and plan their inspections; it cannot set their internal intervals under the current text.

In 2026 PHMSA published a proposed rule that would allow risk-based procedures for breakout tank intervals, with a maximum of 20 years to the first internal inspection and 25 years between later ones, and would require operators to keep records of the likelihood and consequence factors. Until a final rule takes effect, the current section governs. Terminal tanks outside a pipeline system can use API 653's risk-based route within its conditions. None of this is API 580 exam content as such, but it is the kind of boundary a Chicago RBI engineer is asked about weekly.

What the API 580 exam tests, and how to read RP 580 for it

The examination has 90 multiple-choice questions, 80 scored and 10 unscored pretest items, in 3.25 hours, and it is closed-book: no references are available and nothing may be taken in. API reports a scaled score against a set passing mark. The 2026 Body of Knowledge bases the exam on API RP 580, Elements of a Risk-Based Inspection Program, 4th edition (2023) with Addendum 1 (2025), and organises it into ten areas:

  1. terms, definitions and acronyms;
  2. risk assessment;
  3. the RBI programme;
  4. roles, responsibilities, training and qualifications;
  5. data collection;
  6. damage mechanisms;
  7. probability of failure;
  8. consequence of failure;
  9. risk management;
  10. RBI documentation.

Because nothing is open-book, the study task is to know RP 580's vocabulary and logic well enough to choose between four plausible answers without looking anything up. Definitions repay early attention, because many wrong options use a nearby term correctly in the wrong place. Quantitative methods from API RP 581 inform many site programmes, but the exam is built on RP 580's elements, so learn RP 581 only as far as RP 580 refers to it. The API 580 explainer is a short orientation before the course.

A closed-book scenario from an olefins and polymers plant

Picture two items at a plant like the one LyondellBasell runs at Morris, which makes ethylene, propylene and polyethylene. Item A is a carbon steel compressor knock-out drum holding flammable light hydrocarbon gas near an occupied building; its damage is slow and its last inspection was effective, so its probability of failure is low, but a release would be severe. Item B is a cooling water exchanger shell with a history of under-deposit corrosion; its probability of failure is higher, but a leak would release water.

  • Which ranks higher? Possibly A. Risk combines probability and consequence, and a low-probability, high-consequence item can outrank a high-probability, low-consequence one on the matrix.
  • What does more inspection of A achieve? It reduces uncertainty about A's condition and so its probability of failure; it does nothing to the size of a release.
  • What would reduce A's consequence? Measures that limit inventory, speed detection or isolation, or protect the surroundings.
  • What does B need? Possibly a change in cooling water treatment rather than more frequent shell inspection, because the damage driver is the service.

The exam asks this logic in many forms. Candidates who know RP 580's definitions of probability, consequence, inspection effectiveness and risk mitigation answer quickly; candidates who know only their site software's screens struggle.

Studying for API 580 alongside a planning job

API 580 candidates in Chicago usually hold demanding jobs: planners who are busiest in the months before a turnaround, engineers on call for unit upsets, and inspectors who travel between Whiting, Joliet and Gulf Coast sites. Self-paced study fits that. Read RP 580 in short sessions, write your own one-line definition of each term, and send the instructor the questions where your plant's practice and RP 580's wording seem to disagree; working out why is good preparation. Leave the timed practice papers for the final stage, when you can give the full three and a quarter hours to one sitting.

API 580 may be taken at a test centre or, where API offers it for your window, by remote proctoring, which saves a Chicago candidate a drive across the metro. API runs the exam in set windows with application deadlines, listed on the exam schedule page. The certificate lasts three years; you can apply to recertify from 90 days before expiry, a 90-day grace period follows, and employment verification is not currently required.

RBI exam preparation and an RBI study are different jobs

Passing API 580 shows you understand the method; it does not set anyone's inspection intervals. At a plant, the owner's inspection organisation approves intervals and the inspector of record signs for them. Some Chicago-area owners also commission outside assessments, and Atlantis runs remote RBI studies for Chicago-area refineries and terminals as a separate service from this course. Atlantis does not offer fitness-for-service assessment; where an RBI review finds damage that needs one, that work goes to the owner's engineers.

Sponsoring API 580 candidates from a Chicago site

An integrity group often enrols its planners and engineers together, sometimes alongside inspectors preparing for API 510 or 570. One enquiry can cover everyone and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate studies at their own pace, applies to API individually and sits the exam individually, and eligibility is confirmed by API person by person.

faq.q: Must I hold API 510, 570 or 653 to sit API 580 in Chicago?
faq.a: No. A current API 510, 570 or 653 certification qualifies you automatically, but it is not the only route. Without one, API combines education with petrochemical industry experience gained in the last ten years: one year with a bachelor's degree, two with a two-year degree, three with a high school diploma and five or more with no formal education.

faq.q: Does work at a Channahon, Morris or Lemont chemical plant count as petrochemical industry experience?
faq.a: Usually it can, because API's wording for API 580 is petrochemical industry experience rather than inspection under one particular code. Process, reliability, inspection and integrity roles at refineries, olefins and polymer plants and chemical sites are the obvious examples. Describe the work plainly on the application and keep dates and duties ready, because API reviews the experience you list.

faq.q: Does OSHA require RBI at Illinois and Indiana refineries?
faq.a: No. OSHA's process safety management standard requires inspection and testing that follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices, at suitable frequencies, and documented results. RBI is one well-established way to justify those frequencies, not a legal requirement in itself. Federal OSHA enforces the standard for private employers in Illinois, and IOSHA does so in Indiana.

faq.q: Can pipeline breakout tanks at Griffith or Hartsdale use RBI to set internal intervals?
faq.a: Not under the current text of 49 CFR 195.432, which requires API 653 inspections but excludes its risk-based internal interval procedure. RBI can still rank those tanks and plan the work. A 2026 PHMSA proposal would allow RBI for breakout tanks with interval caps, so check whether a final rule has taken effect before relying on either position.

faq.q: Is the API 580 exam open book?
faq.a: No. API 580 is closed-book: no references are available during the examination and nothing may be brought in. It has 90 multiple-choice questions, of which 80 are scored and 10 are unscored pretest items, in 3.25 hours. That is why the course concentrates on RP 580's definitions and reasoning rather than on finding clauses quickly.

faq.q: Will API 580 teach me the RBI software my refinery uses?
faq.a: No. The exam is about the elements of an RBI programme as RP 580 describes them, not about any vendor's software or a site's own risk matrix. Plant software training teaches the screens; exam preparation teaches the concepts behind them. Candidates who know both tend to find the exam questions easier, because they can see what the software is doing.

faq.q: Can I sit API 580 from home instead of driving to a Chicago test centre?
faq.a: Possibly. API 580 may be taken at a test centre or, where API offers it for your window, by remote proctoring. Confirm the delivery options when you apply, because API sets and changes them. API 510, 570 and 653, by contrast, are taken in person at Prometric test centres.

faq.q: After passing API 580, can I approve inspection intervals at my plant?
faq.a: Not on the strength of the certificate alone. Interval approval sits with the owner's inspection organisation under its procedures and with the inspector of record for the equipment. API 580 shows you understand the method behind risk-based intervals, which makes your recommendations more credible, but the decision stays with the people the owner's programme names.
